chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from al-Sayyari, who said: It was narrated from Ibn Abi Layla.

A man brought his adversary to him and said, 'This man sold me this slave girl, but when I uncovered her, I did not find hair on her pubic area, and he claimed she never had any.' Ibn Abi Layla said to him, 'People use tricks in this matter to escape liability; what did you dislike?' He said, 'O Judge, if it is a defect, rule for me on that.' He said, 'Wait until I come out to you, for I feel discomfort in my stomach.' Then he entered and exited through another door and went to Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Thaqafi, and said, 'What do you narrate from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding a woman who does not have hair on her pubic area; is that considered a defect?'

Muhammad ibn Muslim said to him, 'As for this explicitly, I do not know it, but Abu Ja'far narrated to me from his father from his forefathers (peace be upon them) from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) that he said: "Whatever is part of the original creation, if it increases or decreases, it is a defect."' Ibn Abi Layla said, 'That is sufficient for me,' then he returned to the people and ruled in their favor regarding the defect.

key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي لَيْلَى: A prominent judge (Qadi) in early Islamic history
key_terms.عَيْب: Defect or flaw in a sold item
key_terms.مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ مُسْلِم: A companion of the Imams and narrator

ai.seo_question: What constitutes a legal defect in a sale according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the application of the general principle that any deviation from the original state of creation (*asl al-khalq*) constitutes a legal defect (*'ayb*) in commercial transactions. It highlights the scholarly methodology of deriving specific rulings from broad prophetic traditions, as cited by Muhammad ibn Muslim from the Ahl al-Bayt, to resolve disputes over hidden physical attributes in sales.
